title: Tonight
intro: Tonight gives a shared moment value without demanding that it guarantee forever. The moonlit face becomes bridal, but the speaker immediately limits his promise to the present. Another person's presence quiets the outside noise and restores courage. The closing refusal to wait on imaginary possibilities then protects the experience from being measured against a future it never promised. Privacy matters here: something can remain unforgettable because two people know it, without being publicly proved or endlessly prolonged.
reading: Bounded intimacy is valuable without guaranteed permanence; memory can remain while speculative attachment is released.

revisions.t47-n1: The face wears the wedding dress through moonlight, not through an announced ceremony. The image briefly gives the moment the gravity of commitment, then the speaker says he will not think about the future. That sequence keeps the scene from becoming an ordinary proposal song. Ceremonial intensity and limited duration are allowed together: a night can matter deeply without furnishing a contract for what follows.
revisions.editorial-47-present-choice: Refusing to think ahead can sound evasive in another setting, but here it is paired with attending closely to every minute and second. The speaker is trying not to miss the available relationship while imagining a guaranteed one. Later warnings against vain waiting and nonexistent fantasies clarify the choice. The lyric distinguishes treasuring an experience from demanding that it satisfy every possible future wish.
revisions.editorial-47-again-courage: The small word 'again' makes courage a returning capacity, not a permanent possession. Gratitude is therefore substantial without requiring the other person to solve the speaker's entire life. Their presence has made continuing feel possible in this moment. That limited claim fits the song's refusal to convert tonight into a promise of forever, while still allowing it to be consequential.
revisions.editorial-47-past-private: The instruction to let the past pass is followed by an unforgettable experience known only to two people. Forgetting is not required for release. The ending preserves the value of what happened while relinquishing the need to keep it happening or make outsiders validate it. That is a different form of privacy from the defensive secrecy elsewhere on the album: here it shelters shared meaning rather than only guarding against exploitation.
